title: Multiply the Table
subtitle: Five sessions on raising the person you disciple to disciple someone else
summary: Discipleship was never meant to end with you. Paul told Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people who would teach others also, and in one verse he stacked four generations of the faith. This study is five sessions, meant to be walked one on one with the person you have been pouring into, and it aims at a decision. It moves from the command to multiply, to the chain hidden inside a single verse, to the truth that Jesus trained the twelve to be sent and not to stay, to naming the actual next person your disciple could begin to walk with, to the hardest part, letting them go so the table can become two tables. The goal was always the next disciple, never a permanent audience.
setting: The table you have been sitting at, now with an empty chair you are praying God will fill through the person across from you.
forWho: Anyone ready to move from being poured into to pouring out, and the disciple who is ready to become a disciple-maker.
rhythm: Five sessions, one on one, aimed at a decision by the end: who will you take with you next.
leaderNote: A table that never becomes two tables has stopped halfway. The goal of discipleship was always the next disciple, not a permanent audience. Push gently but clearly toward the person your disciple will begin to walk with. Do not rush past the fear, most people who stall at this point are not lazy, they are scared they have nothing to give. Remind them that Paul handed the faith to a young man he called a coward more than once, and it multiplied anyway. Your job by session five is not to have taught everything. It is to have sent someone.

sessions.title: The Command Was Always Multiply
sessions.bigIdea: Paul did not tell Timothy to keep what he learned. He told him to entrust it to faithful people who would teach others also. Discipleship that stops with the disciple was never the plan. The plan was always the next one.
sessions.open: Think back to whoever first walked with you in the faith. What did they hand you that you are still living on today, and have you ever handed it to anyone else?
sessions.read: Read 2 Timothy 2 verse 2 out loud, slowly. And what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
observe: Paul uses the word entrust, the way you hand over something valuable that is not finally yours to keep. What does that word do to the idea that faith is a private possession.
Count how far the verse looks ahead. Timothy is not the end of the sentence. Who is.
talk: You have been on the receiving end of this table for a while now. Be honest, has it started to feel like the point is you, a place to be fed. What would it change to hear that you were being fed in order to feed someone.

Paul says entrust to faithful people. Not the most gifted, not the most impressive, the faithful, the ones who show up and follow through. Who comes to mind when you hear that word, and what makes you hesitate to picture yourself pouring into them.
Where did you get the idea that discipling someone is for experts and pastors and not for you. Name the lie plainly, because it is the thing that will keep this table from ever multiplying.
sessions.practice: This week write down three names, ordinary people you already know who are a step behind you in the faith and would sit down if you asked. Do not decide anything yet. Just let yourself see that the field is not empty.
sessions.send: You were never being filled up to stay full. You were being filled to pour out.
sessions.passItOn: Tell the person who first discipled you that you are starting to think about who comes next. Thank them out loud. A chain only knows it is a chain when someone names the link before them.

sessions.title: Four Generations in One Verse
sessions.bigIdea: Look again at that verse and count the layers. Paul, then Timothy, then faithful people, then others still. Four generations of the faith in a single sentence, and not a program in sight. It is a chain of ordinary people who each handed it on.
sessions.scripture: 2 Timothy 2:2 read again slowly and Matthew 28:19-20
sessions.open: Have you ever seen something good passed down three or four generations in a family, a recipe, a trade, a way of treating people. What kept it alive that long.
sessions.read: Read 2 Timothy 2 verse 2 one more time, and this time count the four generations as you go. And what you have heard from me, that is Paul, the first. In the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, that is Timothy handing it to the second. Who will be able to teach others also, that is the third generation reaching a fourth. Now read Matthew 28 verses 19 and 20. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
observe: In the Matthew passage, the command is not go and make converts. It is make disciples who then observe all that Jesus commanded, which includes this same command to go. Where does the chain repeat inside the sentence.
Paul never met the fourth generation in his verse. He is investing in people he will never see. What does that tell you about what he thought discipleship was for.
talk: A chain and a program are not the same thing. A program can run without love and still fill a room. A chain only moves through relationship, one person who actually knows the next. Which one has this table been, and which one are you being asked to continue.

You are somewhere in a chain that reaches back further than you can see, all the way to a hillside where Jesus said go. That is not a small thing to be part of. How does it change the weight of what you do next to know the line does not stop with you unless you stop it.

Matthew says the command comes with a promise, I am with you always. Most people who never disciple anyone are waiting to feel ready. What would it mean to start before you feel ready, trusting the promise instead of the readiness.
sessions.practice: Draw the chain on paper. Put the name of whoever discipled you, then your name, then a blank line, then another blank line after that. Sit with the two blank lines this week. They are not hypothetical. They are people God already has in mind.
sessions.send: You are not the end of the line. You are the middle of it, and the middle is where the line either continues or dies.
sessions.passItOn: Show your blank-line drawing to the person you are meeting with and let them ask you who might fill the first line. Saying a name out loud to another person is how a maybe becomes a plan.

sessions.title: Sending Is the Goal, Not Keeping
sessions.bigIdea: Jesus called the twelve to be with him, and then to be sent out. The being with was real, but it was never the whole point. He was raising people to send, not an audience to keep. A disciple you never release is a disciple you never finished.
sessions.open: Have you ever held onto something good too long, a job, a role, a season, past the point where letting go would have been the right thing. What made it hard to release.
sessions.read: Read Mark 3 verse 14. And he appointed twelve, whom he also named apostles, so that they might be with him and he might send them out to preach. Notice the two purposes, to be with him, and to be sent. Then read John 20 verse 21, spoken after the resurrection. Jesus said to them again, Peace be with you. As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you.
observe: In Mark, both purposes sit in one breath, with him and sent out. Which one does a lot of us treat as the whole point, and which one gets quietly dropped.
In John, Jesus ties the sending of the disciples to his own sending by the Father. What does it mean that being sent is not a lesser assignment but the same pattern that moved Jesus himself.
talk: It is easy to build a table that people love so much they never leave, and to call that success. But Jesus measured it differently. What is the difference between a disciple who stays comfortable and a disciple who gets sent, and which one have we been aiming at.

There is a real cost to sending. When your disciple starts pouring into someone else, they will have less time for you, and the closeness will change. Say the quiet part out loud, what do you lose when the person across from you gets sent, and why is it still worth it.

Jesus spent three years so that the twelve could carry on without him standing there. If you did your part well, the person you disciple should eventually not need you the same way. Does that feel like loss or like the point. Sit in the honest answer.
sessions.practice: This week, in whatever you and your disciple are already doing together, hand one thing fully over to them. A prayer, a passage to lead, a conversation to start. Do not rescue it if it wobbles. Let them carry it, and watch what being trusted does.
sessions.send: You are not raising someone to sit beside you forever. You are raising someone to be sent.
sessions.passItOn: Ask the person you disciple what they would need from you in order to feel ready to lead someone else. Their answer is your next assignment. Sending starts by preparing them to be sent.

sessions.title: Naming the Next One
sessions.bigIdea: Andrew met Jesus and the very first thing he did was go find his brother Simon and bring him. He did not wait to become an expert. He brought the one person already in front of him. Multiplication almost always starts with a name you already know.
sessions.open: Who is one person already in your life, a family member, a coworker, a neighbor, who is a step behind you and would probably say yes if you offered to walk with them. Do not overthink it. Just say the first name that comes.
sessions.read: Read John 1 verses 40 through 42. One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, We have found the Messiah, which means Christ. He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas, which means Peter.
observe: Andrew had barely followed Jesus himself before he went to get Simon. How much training did Andrew have before he brought someone. What does that free you from.
The person Andrew brought was his own brother, the one closest and most ordinary. Where did the great fisher of men come from. Notice who was standing right next to the disciple already.
talk: Andrew is not the famous brother. Simon Peter is. But Peter is at the table because Andrew went and got him. Most of us underrate the quiet person who simply brings someone. What holds you back from being an Andrew for the name you just said out loud.

You do not need a curriculum or a title to say to someone, would you sit down with me and read the Bible and pray each week. You need a name and a willingness. What is the actual fear underneath not asking, being turned down, not knowing enough, being seen as too spiritual.

Picture yourself six months from now sitting across a table from the person you just named. What would have to happen this month for that picture to become real. Work backward from it right now, together.
sessions.practice: Pick one name and take the first small step this week. Not the whole plan, the first step. A text, a coffee, a simple honest ask. Would you want to walk through some things together for a few weeks. Then tell your discipler what you did and what they said.
sessions.send: The next disciple is not a stranger you have to go find. Most of the time it is a name already standing next to you.
sessions.passItOn: Whoever you name and ask this week is the whole point of this study becoming real. Tell them plainly that someone once did this for you, and now you want to do it for them. Then someday they will say the same words to their someone.

sessions.title: Letting Go So It Grows
sessions.bigIdea: A branch that is never pruned bears less, not more. The Father cuts back the vine precisely so it will bear more fruit, and the church at Antioch laid hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent its two best away. Releasing is not losing. It is how the thing grows.
sessions.open: Have you ever watched something grow better after it was cut back, or after you stepped away from controlling it. What did that teach you that holding on never could.
sessions.read: Read John 15 verses 1 and 2. I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit. Then read Acts 13 verses 2 and 3. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them. Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
observe: In John 15, pruning happens to the branch that is already bearing fruit, not the dead one. Why would the Father cut back a healthy branch. What is he after.
In Acts 13, the church at Antioch sends away Barnabas and Saul, two of its most valuable people. What does it cost a table to release its best, and what came of it for the whole world.
talk: Antioch could have kept Barnabas and Saul and stayed a strong, comfortable church. Instead it fasted, prayed, and gave them away, and the gospel reached the nations because of it. Where are you tempted to keep rather than send, and what might God be waiting to do on the other side of your open hand.

Pruning feels like loss while it is happening. When your disciple gets sent and starts their own table, you will feel the cut. Name it honestly. What will you grieve, and how is that grief actually the evidence that something real grew here.

This is the last session. So make the decision out loud. Who is the next one, when will you begin, and what is the first thing you will do. Say it as a commitment, not a wish, and let the other person hold you to it.
sessions.practice: Before you leave this table, do what Antioch did. Pray over the person you have named to disciple, and pray over your disciple who is about to become a disciple-maker. Lay a hand on a shoulder, say their name, and send them. Then put a date on the calendar for the first meeting of the next table.
sessions.send: The Father prunes what is already fruitful so it will bear more. Open your hand, send them out, and watch one table become two.
sessions.passItOn: This whole study only mattered if it ends in a sending. Do not close it in theory. Set the date, make the ask, and start the next table, so that someday the person you send will sit where you are sitting now and send someone of their own.
